newsitem.title: CHINA: China steps up watch on dissidents in Gore visit.
newsitem.headline: China steps up watch on dissidents in Gore visit.

text.p: China has intensified police surveillance around its tiny community of dissidents to prevent contacts with U.S. officials during the visit of Vice President Al Gore, activists said on Tuesday.
Gore has said he would raise U.S. concerns about treatment of dissidents in China in talks with Chinese officials. He met Premier Li Peng on Tuesday and is to meet President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday.
Gore hinted that he might have raised human rights in his Tuesday morning meeting with Li, referring to areas of disagreement.

"The meetings today were very positive," Gore told reporters as he toured the Forbidden City in the heart of Beijing. "Both sides have a desire to lend forward momentum... recognising areas where we agreed to disagree."
Police in Beijing have told dissidents not to leave their homes during Gore's visit and have stepped up surveillance of their families, activists said.

"Ever since June 1995 there have been police stationed here, watching the door and going wherever I go," said Wang Zhihong, wife of leading pro-democracy activist Chen Ziming who is at home on medical parole while serving a 13-year term for his role in the 1989 student-led demonstrations.
"Now there are twice as many as usual," Wang said by telephone.
"When things are tense they send more people and they follow me more closely. For example if I go shopping they stand right beside me," she said.
"Having people tailing me causes a lot of trouble in my life and work," she added.

Veteran dissident Ren Wanding, released last year after serving a seven-year term for his role in the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations centred in Tiananmen Square has been told to stay at home while Gore is in town, a Hong Kong-based human rights group said.

Local police told Ren to finish his business by Sunday and said he should not go outside from Monday, when Gore started his four-day visit to China, the Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said in a statement.
Police had mounted a 24-hour watch on his movements, the centre said.

Gore is the most senior U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush, who came in early 1989, shortly before the student demonstrations in Beijing that were crushed by the army with heavy loss of life.
China usually intensifies security around its tiny band of dissidents during visits of foreign leaders, especially those interested in China's human rights record.

"I will of course discuss human rights with the leadership of China," Gore said before his arrival. "Nor will it be a surprise to them to have these matters raised...These issues are important to us as Americans because of who we are."

Although Gore has no plans to meet privately with dissidents, officials travelling with him said some Chinese "critics" of government policy had been invited to a Wednesday night dinner at the U.S. embassy.
A sister of China's most prominent dissident, veteran democracy activist Wei Jingsheng, has appealed to Gore to ask Chinese leaders to free him from a 14-year jail term.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
